sub_answers.text: He severed relations with the UWFi when the company started moving away from its shootfighting style and favoring performers over wrestlers [d668815s10p0]. He publicly criticized the promotion's use of power bombs as unrealistic despite their use by others and in MMA [d668815s10p0]. He was highly critical of modern professional wrestling, describing it as "choreographed tumbling" that showcased little real wrestling skill [d668815s10p0].

sub_answers.text: His coaches taught submission wrestling and techniques for wrestling from the bottom, shaping trainees' grappling fundamentals and resilience in matches [d668815s3p0]. His intensive study under Ad Santel developed trainees into very dangerous grapplers, influencing a more submission- and catch-oriented in-ring style [d668815s3p0]. His trainers also taught extremely painful and potentially crippling submission holds that became part of trainees' repertoire for overcoming opponents who refused to lose [d668815s3p0].

sub_answers.text: Louis, who taught him submission wrestling and how to wrestle from the bottom [d668815s3p0]. He studied intensively under catch wrestler Ad Santel for up to five days every week during a six-month stay in California and returned to train under Santel whenever he was in the area [d668815s3p0]. He was mentored and later managed by Ed "Strangler" Lewis, who taught him painful submission holds and served as a trainer figure [d668815s3p0]. In later years he served as a trainer and head coach himself — holding seminars, acting as commission/occasional trainer for UWFi in Japan, and heading CACC Snake Pit Japan — demonstrating formal coaching roles and repeated instructional engagements [d668815s10p0][d668815s0p0].
